<reason>PRO opened with a compelling structural frame (defaults vs. willpower, equity, "turn off the current") and closed on a memorable coverage argument. But CON did more damage across the exchange: it grounded its case in plausible, well-known real-world deployments (Denmark, Mexico, UK levy, Chile, Quebec), caught PRO listing calorie labeling as its own tool and then disowning it, and used its pressure question to extract an explicit concession that no jurisdiction has reduced obesity via the environmental approach. CON also answered PRO's pressure questions squarely (same three-year weight window for DPP-style programs; schools as a universal, non-income-gated default; regressivity of soda taxes). PRO never addressed the school-based default or the regressivity point, and its final "in the people they reach" framing was turned around by CON's "universal coverage of a null effect is not reach." CON's two clipped turns are a minor execution cost but do not offset its cleaner control of the decisive clash on measured outcomes versus coverage.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B3.1/A4.1/B4.5 sequence: CON demanded one jurisdiction where environmental policy reduced obesity; PRO conceded none exists and tried to make it symmetric; CON answered that its programs have moved weight in those reached and that schools reach every child, leaving PRO's coverage argument without an unanswered mechanism.</best_rebuttal>
